newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli official quits over scandal probe results.
newsitem.headline: Israeli official quits over scandal probe results.

text.p: Israel's deputy finance minister said on Wednesday he was quitting over the findings of a corruption investigation into Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government and would try to persuade others to join him.

David Magen, of Foreign Minister David Levy's Gesher faction, told Reuters he had considered quitting his post for weeks but Netanyahu's response to a report 10 days ago by public prosecutors was the last straw.

Netanyahu lashed out at the media and opposition in a speech only moments after prosecutors, citing insufficient evidence, had decided not to charge him. Prosecutors however said there were "real suspicions" about his role in the scandal.

"The straw that broke the camel's back was the prime minister's horror show on television following publication of the decision," said Magen, whose faction is part of a right-wing bloc with Netanyahu's Likud party.

"The reasons for my resignation, which have to do with political and parliamentary developments I foresee, will be explained at a later date in the proper framework," he said in a letter obtained by Reuters.

Police who conducted the corruption investigation had recommended indicting Netanyahu, Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi, Netanyahu's director-general Avigdor Lieberman and key legislator Aryeh Deri in connection with the short-lived appointment in January of Likud political crony Roni Bar-On as attorney-general.
Prosecutors announced a 75-page decision to charge Deri alone but petitioners have asked the High Court of Justice to order indictments against the prime minister.

Netanyahu admitted making mistakes in the appointment, which Channel One Television alleged was part of a plea-bargain deal for Deri already on trial for corruption. But Netanyahu said he had been vindicated of any criminal act.

"At base the attacks against me come from one central motive: an attempt to overthrow the government because of our opponents' fundamental disagreement with our path," Netanyahu said after the prosecutors' decision.
"They refuse to accept the fact that the people voted for us and not for them," the Israeli leader said.
Magen, who remains in Israel's parliament, said he would meet Levy to urge him and others in their five-member Gesher faction to bolt the government and try to bring about early elections.
Gesher's departure could shake Netanyahu's 66-member coalition but there were no signs Levy or other legislators would join Magen.
